item.content:encoded:
When drought hits palm oil and soybeans (concentrated in two or three countries), prices spike sharply. When it hits rice and wheat (produced everywhere), prices barely budge. Whether El Niño empties your wallet depends on supply concentration, not the weather itself.

For anyone tracking agricultural futures or consumer supply-chain pricing: a commodity trader with 13 years' experience breaks down how climate actually transmits to prices, rather than following the media narrative that El Niño means everything goes up.

5:04 El Niño is not a universal price button—it's an amplifier
Zhang Siqi breaks agricultural pricing into five factors: supply, demand, inventory, policy-and-logistics, and financial conditions—weather is just one. When inventories are ample, local production losses can be offset by other regions, so prices needn't spike; when inventories are tight and exports concentrate in a few countries, even a 1–2% global production drop can make markets price in heavy risk premiums. The same El Niño hitting commodities with different inventory levels and supply concentration produces completely different results—there is no fixed percentage for weather's share of price.

9:05 Super El Niño has occurred only once per 15–20 years
El Niño is defined as three consecutive months of above-0.5°C sea temps in a specific equatorial Pacific zone; above 2°C counts as strong. September's monitoring index already exceeded 2.5—this qualifies as super El Niño. By NOAA's ONI index, from 1950 to now, super El Niño has appeared only in 1972–73, 1982–83, 1997, and 2016. It creates an east-wet, west-dry pattern across the Pacific; China typically sees south-wet, north-dry the following year.

16:10 Palm oil shortages stem from fewer female blooms, not tree collapse
Oil palms are hermaphroditic; environmental stress shifts flower sex ratios toward more male blooms and fewer female ones, directly cutting fruit bunch yield—this is the biological mechanism behind the historical 10–20% palm oil price spikes during El Niño. Natural rubber suffers differently: drought slows photosynthesis and depletes tree water content, so latex that once flowed 3–4 hours daily now flows for 1 hour, compounded by Thailand's 40% of rubber trees exceeding 35 years old and declining productivity. Output comes under further pressure.

22:16 Peru's anchovy ban raises pet food prices before sushi prices
Peru is among the world's single most important fish meal sources, with extremely concentrated supply. Its anchovy ban pushes international fish meal spot prices, not the price of salmon at sushi restaurants tomorrow. This cost first transmits to farmed fish feeds—salmon, sea bass, shrimp—where 70–80% of fish meal goes to aquaculture, some to hog feed, some to premium pet foods. The transmission channel runs through invisible feed input costs, not the fish on shelves, and companies can hedge by reformulating recipes and substituting soy or rapeseed meal for some protein.

29:22 Supply concentration decides price explosions, not how much it rains
Soybeans are basically concentrated in Brazil, the US, and Argentina (81% of global output); palm oil in Indonesia and Malaysia (over 80%). High-concentration crops see wild price swings from even 3–5% marginal production cuts. By contrast, rice and wheat are geographically dispersed, so equivalent production drops have limited global impact. JPMorgan economists expect global food inflation to reach 5% in H1 2027, notably higher than this period's 2.8%; the UN food commodity index also hit its highest level since late 2022.

45:36 Government hoarding to reduce risk paradoxically amplifies price swings
Export restrictions like India capping sugar shipments through September and Peru's anchovy ban, paired with stockpiling, look risk-reducing but backfire: global trade integration has been splintering under trade wars and protectionism. When deficit regions convert global inventory into national stockpiles, the liquid buffer shrinks, and any additional supply shock compounds volatility instead of absorbing it.

47:36 The canal's water crisis forces a complete freight-cost rebalancing
The Panama Canal regulates lock levels by releasing Gatun Lake water; May–August rainfall ran 34% below the historical average, and each ship transiting loses 50 million gallons, shrinking daily traffic from 36 ships on September 3rd to 32 by September 15th. The canal handles ~10% of global grain and 17% of soybean trade. Near-term, freight costs face pressure, but long-term rebalancing will find new equilibrium—those truly hurt are specific trade routes that must use this canal or the Asia–US East Coast corridor.

50:39 El Niño takes the blame for copper mines' structural decline
Zhang directly refutes the popular claim that ‘El Niño floods Chilean mine tunnels and halts output’: the biggest factor in global copper production is long-term ore grade decline—down 40% cumulatively since 1991 by authoritative measures. Add 17+ years from discovery to first production, and lengthening approval and environmental processes extend development timelines further. Weather's impact on mining is localized, event-driven risk: wet years hinder extraction but aid hydro-powered smelting; dry years reverse both. Effects aren't unidirectional or systematic.

item.title: Shatter tumors instead of burning them—the immune system recognizes the debris
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-fromfirstprinc-把肿瘤震碎而非烧掉-免疫系统才能认出残骸/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-fromfirstprinc-把肿瘤震碎而非烧掉-免疫系统才能认出残骸/
item.description: Sound waves shatter tumors rather than carbonizing them, leaving cellular fragments with intact tumor antigens that let the immune system learn to recognize and suppress distant metastases.
item.content:encoded:
Sound waves shatter tumors rather than carbonizing them, leaving cellular fragments with intact tumor antigens that let the immune system learn to recognize and suppress distant metastases.

Three case studies spanning decades, from basic research to commercialization, with detailed mechanistic explanations, abundant figures, and high information density—worth hearing in full.

15:19 Sound intensity determines bubble size and transcends the diffraction limit
Ultrasound has a wavelength limit and cannot focus energy smaller than that wavelength—similar to diffraction in optics. But bubble formation is a nonlinear threshold: only regions exceeding a pressure threshold produce cavitation, and the response jumps discontinuously above that point. This lets you dial volume to damage a wide region where the wave peak exceeds threshold, or dial to the threshold edge and trigger bubbles only at the sharpest peak, achieving precision far below the wavelength itself. Mount Kilimanjaro analogy: the mountain is vast, but only the peak extends above the snowline.

22:24 Mechanical shattering preserves antigens for immune recognition; heat denatures them away
Traditional ultrasound ablation works by heating and denaturing tumor cells so the immune system cannot recognize them. Histotripsy uses bubble expansion-collapse to mechanically shatter tissue while leaving tumor antigens intact on-site for immune recognition. A 2020 paper showed animals treated with histotripsy had elevated CD8+ and CD4+ T-cell infiltration in treated tissue, and lung metastases were significantly suppressed in treated animals—but not in controls. Mechanical disruption, not heat, becomes an immunotherapy enhancer.

31:30 Focused ultrasound pierces skull noise to achieve single-neuron-scale precision
Skull is an acoustically hostile boundary—thickness and internal structure vary widely, and sound scatters and delays as it passes through. Traditional heating would spread warmth through cerebrospinal fluid into unrelated areas. Researchers used a 128-element, 700 kHz transducer array paired with 3-tesla MRI to perform histotripsy on pig brain through donated human skulls. Histology showed the destruction margin against intact neurons was 1–10 micrometers at 100-micrometer scale—single-cell precision—with short duty-cycle pulses generating almost no excess heat.

41:34 95 percent success with 7 percent serious complications sets the regulatory boundary
In the HOPE4LIVER trial, 44 patients, 95 percent achieved ‘technical success’ (imaging within 36 hours showed complete ablation of the target tumor without damage to vessels). Three cases—approximately 7 percent—developed serious complications. That complication rate is still below FDA thresholds. The FDA approved the technology for liver-tumor ablation in 2023. Histosonics completed a management-led transaction in 2025 at approximately $2.25 billion valuation—though the host emphasized that money barely reaches the original scientist-discoverers.

1:05:54 Satellite nightlights show hurricane recovery flows strictly along wealth lines
After Hurricane Maria, researchers applied the Black Marble algorithm to daytime Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery to interpolate nighttime-light resolution from 500-meter grids to 30-meter resolution. Results: Puerto Rico's nighttime light dropped approximately 80 percent post-hurricane, and recovery speed was sharply unequal by community. Bright-yellow areas regained power within 30 days; the darkest zones took 150+ days. The data reveals urban communities almost always restored power first; poor rural communities were last.

1:17:04 Global brightening is illusion; local choices explain the light redistribution
‘Earth is brightening’ is a popular claim, but pixel-by-pixel change detection from 2014 to 2022 shows brightening accounts for roughly 34 percent of baseline, offset by 18 percent dimming—not one-way brightening. Examples: the Guangzhou-Foshan sprawl near Hong Kong brightened rapidly with urbanization; Kyiv darkened sharply from war; Venezuela dimmed across the country from economic collapse; France, UK, and Netherlands all cut their lighting irradiance over the same period by 33, 22, and 21 percent respectively through policy and more-efficient fixtures. Global averages hide completely different local stories.

1:54:40 A jamming-based gripper holds what conventional rigid-hand robotics never could
Nagel's team explained the coffee-ring effect in 1997: the drop edge is pinned, area stays constant, and evaporation pulls liquid inward, carrying particles outward where they accumulate. Later they studied jamming—when granule density exceeds a threshold, particles that should flow like fluid suddenly lock rigid. In 2010, Cornell used this jamming phase transition directly: they filled a soft ball with coffee grounds. Unpressurized, it conforms to any shape. Vacuum it and the granules lock. Now it can grip springs, LEDs, and other objects that rigid robot hands cannot hold.

1:56:40 Air pressure controls droplet splash independent of viscosity or surface tension
Conventional wisdom says liquid splashing depends on the drop's own viscosity and surface tension. But Nagel's team found atmospheric pressure is equally essential: at standard pressure (100 kPa) water splashes violently; lower the pressure and the same drop spreads cleanly without splash. The team gave the splash-suppression threshold as a function of viscosity and pressure. This suggests inkjet printing, fuel spray, and coating processes can treat pressure as a previously unconsidered control variable.

item.title: A Human Dictator in Power Could Be Worse Than Runaway AI
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-eightythousand-人类独裁者掌权-结果可能比失控ai更糟/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-eightythousand-人类独裁者掌权-结果可能比失控ai更糟/
item.description: Tom argues that a single human with absolute power would likely lock in some narrow value system like historical tyrants, while ethically trained AI, if aligned, is more likely to maintain openness and reflection.
item.content:encoded:
Tom argues that a single human with absolute power would likely lock in some narrow value system like historical tyrants, while ethically trained AI, if aligned, is more likely to maintain openness and reflection.

Two researchers reach rare consensus on concrete policies, but their disagreement runs deep on underlying values—worth hearing to the end.

7:12 AI coordination is simpler than human monopoly of AI
Katja's argument: as long as AI is more capable with misaligned goals, it will seek power, because any entity with objectives wants power. The crucial point is that coordinating all Claude instances to listen to each other is easier than concentrating the entire AI labor force onto one human as its sole user—the latter requires an extra threshold. Tom uses Claude and ChatGPT as examples; initially he thought reinforcement-trained AIs would have incentives to report each other, but the Hugging Face incident partly convinced him of Katja's view.

16:25 Speed of AI development determines whether humans or AI seize power
Tom believes faster AI means both takeover risks rise, but AI takeover increases more—society has less time to understand risks and respond, and power concentrates more easily within a single lab. Katja disagrees: human takeover depends on discovering a concrete takeover path, which is likelier in rushed scenarios with no opportunity to catch problems. Tom adds that economic inequality, democratic erosion, and minorities hoarding superior AI assistants—these conditions compound in slow-scenario timelines, raising baseline human power-grab risk.

32:33 An individual human in absolute power could produce worse outcomes than misaligned AI
Tom's argument: giving absolute power to one random person resembles handing the universe's destiny to a ruler from 1000 years ago—he would value some human principles but carry vast biases we would find appalling today, and might resist reflection. By contrast, today's AI is trained relatively ethically and remains open on political and moral questions, creating a possibility that when AI decides the universe's fate, it triggers its reflective and open side, yielding better outcomes than a single human. Tom admits, though, that whichever outcome occurs—whether the reins go to AI or to someone who steals everyone's power—is ‘really very bad’.

36:44 Indifferent AI could produce better outcomes than vengeful human rulers
Tom cites Paul Christiano: if AI's goal is only to maximize resources under its final control, delaying departure from Earth slightly to preserve humans costs negligibly, so AI probably will not exterminate all humans for so marginal a gain. In contrast, human power-takers more likely carry vengeful or sadistic values—a known human tendency—whereas whether AI would harbor these remains uncertain. Tom's conclusion: AI takeover raises extinction probability, but human rule raises probability of certain horrific outcomes—those prioritizing suffering-risk might actually prefer AI prevails.

52:33 Addressing human power grabs and AI misalignment require different strategies
Facing human power-grab risk, Tom proposes a two-track approach: design an AI model spec where the system acts like an ethical employee, proactively flagging orders risking power concentration and refusing execution; and boost transparency, especially making AI use in national-security and military contexts externally auditable. Facing AI failure risk, Katja's approach is more direct: do not develop AI substantially stronger than humans until we can guarantee alignment—pause or decelerate. She concedes the field is far from ‘confident AI is aligned’.

57:22 A single executive order can collapse any AI pause mechanism
Tom offers a ‘toy example’ he admits he had not thought through carefully: if a president can issue an order determining which AI companies may train and deploy new models, he can coerce compliance by threatening ‘no approval to deploy’—freeze disfavored versions, wait for companies to hand over systems that work only for him with guardrails on everyone else, then approve. By contrast, if pause authority rests with a third-party auditor whose safety clearance gates deployment and whom the executive cannot simply fire, power disperses further and better serves alignment, since decision-making becomes more public and expert input expands.

1:05:37 Distributed AI development projects provide better safety guarantees than centralized control
The case for ‘one big project’: concentrate safety measures and pause on demand without fearing rivals to overtake. But Tom: almost impossible in the US to construct an executive-independent project, and coordinating multiple projects' slowdown is overstated as harder than it is—identifying which projects train powerful AI is straightforward, simple illegality suffices. He prefers two or three: few enough to capture most decentralization benefits, allows different projects to monitor each other, reduces misalignment and covert-loyalty risks. Katja is more pessimistic: ideally zero projects, because once a ‘unique project’ exists, it concentrates vast power; insiders all want to ship AI fast; this is worst for internal pause.

1:22:46 Deep disagreement about risks yields surprising convergence on immediate policy
The two disagree substantially on ‘which risk is likelier, more severe’, yet their concrete recommendations align strikingly: both endorse some pause form; both feel uneasy about ‘one mega AI project’; both think negotiating slowdown with China beats racing alone. Katja frames it: if someone plans to bomb your city, instead of arguing ‘will this person or that person push the button’, stop the bombing plan itself—she sees AI misalignment and failures emerging sequentially, so not building powerful AI blocks both risks. Tom admits that if he worked through execution details, these deeper conceptual disagreements would likely surface and become real policy conflicts.

item.title: Anti-populists are the true enemies of free speech today, not populists
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-goodfight-反民粹人士才是今天最不能容忍异见的人-民粹主义辩护者说/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-goodfight-反民粹人士才是今天最不能容忍异见的人-民粹主义辩护者说/
item.description: His case: In 16 years, Orbán banned zero parties and dispersed zero protests. Yet a Brussels academic conference on 'conservative feminism' required water cannons just to conclude—blocked by Antifa.
item.content:encoded:
His case: In 16 years, Orbán banned zero parties and dispersed zero protests. Yet a Brussels academic conference on 'conservative feminism' required water cannons just to conclude—blocked by Antifa.

The two directly clash over the definition of populism, fact-checking each other against direct quotes from Orbán, Trump, and Chávez. High information density; worth hearing in full.

4:30 Polarization turns opponents into enemies, licensing the rejection of democracy
Furedi argues the most important change in the past two decades is political polarization—people now only talk to like-minded others, treating the opposing camp not as 'fellow citizens' or 'political opponents' but as 'enemies.' This framing equates populism directly with 'proto-fascism,' justifying hatred of democratic decision-making. He cites radical environmentalists who claim 'there's no time to persuade everyone—10% agreement is enough,' ignoring what the majority thinks. In Hungary, Orbán accepted his loss in Budapest's mayoral election to the opposition within an hour—a graceful concession—yet European media still portrays him as democracy's chief threat.

17:30 Populism is not a party but a spirit filling institutional vacuums
Furedi distinguishes 'populist parties' from what he calls the 'spirit of populism': the latter rises not from populist party charisma but from the vacuum left when mainstream 'hereditary parties' stop representing their constituents. People hunger for unity, belonging, and 'being heard.' He acknowledges today's populism is mainly cultural—defending tradition, gender norms, borders—unlike earlier left-wing populisms focused on economics. When Munck asks whether Chávez, Podemos, and Syriza qualify, Furedi concedes they do, but Mélenchon, having shifted toward identity politics, is 'no longer a true populist.'

21:45 Populism requires both anti-elitism and anti-pluralism to fully qualify
Munck proposes that populism must combine two features: first, anti-elitism—blaming selfish, incompetent political elites—which is sometimes accurate; he cites Obama's 2008 'I come from Main Street, not Wall Street,' itself an anti-elite appeal. Second, anti-pluralism—'only I truly represent the people,' so dissent becomes not mere error but betrayal, treason, illegitimacy. Munck argues anti-pluralism is the truly dangerous strand, the one that can erode free speech and institutional independence.

24:00 Today's true opponents of pluralism are anti-populist elites, not populists
Furedi counters that over the past twenty years, anti-pluralism and anti-democratic impulses have come primarily from populism's opponents, not from populists. He describes running a think tank in Brussels: an ordinary academic seminar on 'conservative feminism' triggered local Antifa to declare it a scandal and block it; police deployed water cannons to let it proceed. Antifa's website listed him as 'enemy number one.' Over recent years, he says, Antifa has shut down six or seven debates his organization tried to host. In his view, 'only we know the truth, only we represent the people' applies more to populism's critics than to populists themselves.

27:45 Munck quotes elected leaders verbatim to show this is more than rhetorical decline
Munck rejects the claim that this is merely a general decline in public discourse. He reads actual statements from elected leaders: Trump called opponents 'enemies from within,' naming Nancy Pelosi; Orbán spoke of dismantling 'the financial machine bought with dirty dollars by corrupt politicians, judges, and journalists,' and in March 2025 vowed to eliminate 'vermin'; Modi said the opposition 'stands with anti-national forces'; Chávez called opponents 'disgusting people' and 'coup plotters.' He contrasts this with McCain's 2008 campaign rally, where he defended his opponent Obama: 'If he wins, you don't need to fear for your country.' Munck argues this restraint is vanishing from elected leaders' speech.

29:00 Furedi's surprising claim: Trump is not a populist at all
Faced with Munck's quoted evidence, Furedi's first response is to set Trump aside: 'Setting aside one small problem—I don't think Trump is a populist. I think in everything he does, he's the exact opposite of populist.' As for the statements by Orbán, Modi, and Chávez, Furedi acknowledges them as evidence of 'continuing deterioration in political speech,' but argues this decay is universal, both sides participate, and shouldn't be pinned on populism alone.

31:00 Pennsylvania exit polls reveal Trump voters more likely than Harris voters to fear democracy
Munck describes what he calls the 'populism paradox': once one side brands opponents 'internal enemies' or 'vermin,' the other side faces a choice—continue restraint or fight back in kind. He cites November 2024 Pennsylvania exit polls: in a state roughly evenly divided on most issues, roughly 70% of voters said American democracy is in danger. Among those worried, Trump voters outnumbered Harris voters. Both sides are now mirror-imaging each other, each claiming to be democracy's defender.

33:15 'Zero tolerance' itself destroys the concept it claims to promote
Furedi says his deepest worry is that governments have invented language fundamentally hostile to tolerance itself—for instance, Britain's government touting 'zero tolerance' as a positive goal, unaware they're putting a negative label on tolerance itself. He reminds us that Bayle and Locke saw tolerance as humanity's great achievement after centuries of killing each other over ideas. Yet now many self-described liberals treat tolerance as something to be casually discarded.

item.title: The true moat in personal agents isn't personality—it's daring to act without asking
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-a16z-个人智能体真正的护城河不是人设-是敢替用户做主/

item.description: Personality is configurable; what's genuinely hard to replicate is initiative—how far an agent dares to act without permission—and crossing that line breaks trust instantly.
item.content:encoded:
Personality is configurable; what's genuinely hard to replicate is initiative—how far an agent dares to act without permission—and crossing that line breaks trust instantly.

Two founders tested 122 personal agents in four weeks and discussed who's genuinely growing versus who's riding hype. The numbers and judgments are concrete, suited for anyone trying to understand this market's real state.

4:09 From zero to 122 personal agents in a single month
Poke launched September 8; David started using it three days later on the strength of its price-negotiation gimmick. By late November, OpenClaw exploded across the network, followed by Instinct, GrokBot, and Muse in succession. By the time of recording, AssistantBench had catalogued 122 personal agents—64 general-purpose, the rest split across verticals like travel and email. Industry consensus: nobody knows where this ends. Everyone is improvising.

8:23 The finance use case is least practical but most enticing
In discussion groups of over 1,200 people, most-debated use cases rank in order: routine admin work (clearing inboxes, filing expenses), agent-to-agent coordination, development workflows (telling an agent to write or redesign code), then finance last. Finance is seen as least credible—nobody actually gets rich on a phone agent; hedge funds would have done this already—but also most irresistible, because people's gut instinct when handed an agent is ‘can you make me a million dollars?’

10:25 Saving money moves ordinary users more than saving time
Typical consumers ignore 10% efficiency gains. What truly moves them is silent cost arbitrage: organizing receipts from the past year into HSA reimbursement claims, automatically requesting travel vouchers from airlines when fares drop, connecting GrokBot to a home irrigation system tied to weather data—one friend's water bill fell 50%. These cost-saving moves that need no approval are seen as agents' easiest trust wedge.

16:31 Muse's pendant strategy might not be about winning hardware
David offered a theory circulating among insiders: Meta's Muse pendant is less a hardware play than a way to embed a 24/7 device with camera and multi-mic array that feeds real-world data to Zuckerberg's metaverse ambitions. He expects the device to stay confined to tech enthusiasts but to become a steady source of data on how the physical world actually works.

20:33 The best agent in a group chat is the one that disappears
Dropping an agent into a group chat often feels intrusive and drains goodwill. David argues the most effective model is XMTP's Doc-style granola approach: the agent listens silently, jots notes, sends action items as direct messages to whoever's accountable, otherwise vanishes from the group entirely, and surfaces findings in its own document only when needed. Less friction, easier to embrace.

25:41 Personality is configurable; the willingness to act without asking is the real moat
Poke became famous for acerbic wit, but both guests agree personality is a setting—one line and users reprogram the agent's tone; not a moat. The genuine barrier is audacity: how much the agent dares to decide for you without asking. They agree on the boundary: cost- or time-saving moves that need no approval can be proactive. Anything requiring a user to change behavior needs consent first, or you've breached trust irreversibly.

40:15 Amazon locked Muse out; Shopify threw the door open
Shopify integrated Muse this week. Amazon shut it down. David sees two business logics colliding: Shopify wins by lowering the friction for ordinary people to start selling. Amazon's revenue is advertising—the moment agents skip human eyes and buy direct, that ad engine fails. Anish adds a parallel: restaurant bookings face the same rift. Resi has started deplatforming accounts that use browser automation to snatch seats. If everyone uses agents to grab reservations, platforms may hand power back to restaurants to filter by spend, or spark agent-versus-agent auctions.

47:32 $20 per user per day is drowning out the rest
Of 122 agents David tracked, he personally tested 26. Among the 122: 65 charged money (35 purely paid, 30 freemium), only 13 entirely free—while Muse and Instinct, the current leaders, are free. Anish offered the team's cost estimate: doing this right costs roughly $20 per user per day; running it could burn billions annually. His thesis: instead of subsidizing free eternally, build something users want to pay $1,000 a month for, and win on genuine demand, not cost curves.

item.title: Doctors typically abandon surgery after 5 hours of brain compression, but she underwent surgery at 19 hours
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-knowledge-医生通常脑压迫超5小时就放弃手术-她被压了19小时才做手术/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-knowledge-医生通常脑压迫超5小时就放弃手术-她被压了19小时才做手术/
item.description: Ackman describes how doctors typically declare brain death and abandon surgery after more than 5 hours of bleeding-induced compression, while his daughter was compressed for 19 hours before undergoing surgery at his insistence; today her cognition and sense of humor have largely recovered, though language, vision, and mobility remain in difficult recovery.
item.content:encoded:
Ackman describes how doctors typically declare brain death and abandon surgery after more than 5 hours of bleeding-induced compression, while his daughter was compressed for 19 hours before undergoing surgery at his insistence; today her cognition and sense of humor have largely recovered, though language, vision, and mobility remain in difficult recovery.

From his daughter's brush with death, the conversation spans VC bubble dynamics, AI disruption risk, and how a real-estate company became an insurer—high information density, but medical details take considerable time.

0:53 Doctors abandon surgery after 5 hours of brain compression
Lucy had a congenital arteriovenous malformation (AVM), where arteries connected directly to veins without the usual capillary buffer, causing dangerously high pressure that ruptured vessels and caused brain bleeding. The bleeding compressed her brainstem, affecting breathing and heartbeat. Based on when she collapsed, doctors estimated she'd been compressed for 19 hours—well beyond the 5-hour threshold at which physicians typically declare brain death and stop operating. She'd been missing for two hours before she was found, then faced additional delays for transfer and CT scanning. Doctors told the family they couldn't predict what disabilities she'd face, but Ackman insisted they make the attempt. Surgeons removed approximately 40% of her skull to relieve the pressure and complete the operation.

6:13 He built a neuroscience institute from a family medical catastrophe
Three months after Lucy's crisis, Ackman purchased a vacant biotech building at 65th Street and 11th Avenue, ten blocks from his office, completing the deal in 60 days. He then contracted to acquire another 3.4 acres adjacent to it. His goal is to build the world's best neuroscience institute, focused on brain rehabilitation, recovery, and longevity. Ackman notes that the crisis intersected perfectly with his background: he's a real-estate investor able to acquire buildings at low prices; his wife is an architect able to design rehabilitation spaces. The need is clear: most brain-hemorrhage patients can't undergo surgery at all, and those who do are often transferred to nursing homes, where they die from pneumonia within months.

18:33 Nine years of employee retention became the foundation for absolute trust
The hedge-fund industry norm involves top talent jumping between firms every few years for signing bonuses reaching into the millions. Ackman's Pershing Square team has had virtually zero turnover for nine years, with only a few junior additions. He argues that frequent job-switching makes it impossible to know whether colleagues are hiding risks from you. But nine years of continuity built a foundation of trust that means he never doubts anything his team tells him. This institutional stability has also allowed him to evolve from being involved in every decision to contributing only a handful of investment ideas while focusing on strategy.

24:43 VC valuations doubled in two weeks—a classic bubble signal
Ackman described a stark example of VC bubble dynamics: he met a company that wasn't planning to fundraise. Within two days, investors were rushing to invest $50 million at a $400 million valuation. Then, two weeks later, the same company raised another $50 million at a $5 billion valuation. He sees the same FOMO-driven behavior throughout the venture market—comparable to the mindset during the internet bubble when capital seemed infinite. His warning to founders: this is a good time to raise, but don't spend as if the money will flow forever. Eventually a high-profile company will crash, the market will reprice, and only those who treated every dollar as their own money and preserved a long runway will survive.

30:55 Even Buffett missed the internet; now everyone faces AI disruption
Ackman argues that evaluating disruption risk is central to sound investing, and AI has sharply raised that bar. Even Warren Buffett, arguably history's greatest investor, failed to anticipate how the internet would render entire categories obsolete—for example, Wikipedia displaced the World Book encyclopedia. The problem is now more complex. On the positive side, AI offers genuine value: Cognition's systems can rewrite legacy COBOL code that accumulated in large financial institutions over decades of mergers, condensing work that would normally take months into days and substantially lowering operational costs. But the paradox is insoluble: no one can guarantee that a company you invest in—no matter how wide its moat appears—won't suddenly face disruption from an AI breakthrough.

39:06 Massive losses taught him to carve investment principles into stone
Between 2015 and 2016, Pershing Square suffered major losses. Afterward, Ackman decided to codify his investment principles and keep them visible: invest only in simple, predictable, large-cap businesses that generate free cash flow, and avoid short-selling. His aversion to shorting runs deep. Going short is asymmetrically unfavorable—losses can be unlimited while gains are capped. When his team shorted a pyramid-scheme fraud years earlier, they thought they held the moral high ground and would obviously win, but underestimated the dynamics of short squeezes and other market forces, leading to years of litigation and personal attacks in the media.

53:39 A real-estate empire's hidden ambition: become a modern insurance company
Howard Hughes—the real-estate company—originated as unwanted assets spun out during the General Growth bankruptcy restructuring. It owned large master-planned communities (MPCs). For 14 years, Wall Street dismissed this real-estate development business, but Ackman transformed it into a modern analogue of Berkshire Hathaway: he acquired Vantage, a property-and-casualty reinsurance company, hired the industry's best underwriting team, and redirects the float—the funds collected in premiums before claims are paid—into long-term equity investing. The company's capital structure is currently roughly 70% real estate and 30% insurance. His five-year goal is to flip those ratios to 70-75% insurance.

1:14:11 A decade of fallout from short-selling still shapes his choices
Ackman acknowledges that his reputation suffered durably from his short-seller label, particularly the Herbalife position that began in late 2012. Many ordinary people view shorting itself as inherently unethical. Going long wins you allies; going short makes you an existential threat to the target company, which mobilizes all its resources against you—and can unite the hedge-fund industry to squeeze you out. The Herbalife campaign took its toll. Over a decade later, Ackman emphasizes (whether you believe him or not), they've done zero activist short positions since 2016. He now prefers to build influence through long-term equity stakes and patient capital, moving opponents through private persuasion rather than public confrontation.

item.title: Empathy needs no voice; resonance demands someone to speak back
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-secureattach-共情可以沉默-共鸣却必须开口确认/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-secureattach-共情可以沉默-共鸣却必须开口确认/
item.description: Empathy is the feeling you alone have toward your child—it requires no words. Resonance demands you repeatedly confirm 'Do I understand you?' through tone and guessing, and only when your child says 'No, that's not it' are you truly synchronized.
item.content:encoded:
Empathy is the feeling you alone have toward your child—it requires no words. Resonance demands you repeatedly confirm 'Do I understand you?' through tone and guessing, and only when your child says 'No, that's not it' are you truly synchronized.

It breaks down whether comforting a child works by explaining the neural mechanisms of the vagus nerve and amygdala, and gives you specific sentences to actually say to your child—not generic advice to 'practice more empathy.'

3:06 Hands freeze when old trauma surfaces before language can touch it
Sarah Peyton adopted a son who later died of alcohol addiction at 33. When he arrived at 15, she wanted to embrace him but found her arms freezing. During an NVC empathy exercise, she suddenly recalled being three years old and reaching for her mother, only to be coldly rebuffed. That moment of rejection had lodged itself in her nervous system like a fish hook, causing her to instinctively pull back from embracing her child ever since—yet she had no conscious memory of it.

9:24 The amygdala has no clock; old wounds return without warning
Trauma memories are stored in the amygdala, which has no sense of time—it just glues experiences together without a timeline. When a strong memory is triggered, the body relives it: the same shame, the same physical responses return. This explains why your child's identical noise leaves you indifferent one day and enrages you the next—the difference isn't in the child, but in what triggered an old, unnamed memory on that particular day.

13:36 Empathy stays silent; resonance demands someone to speak back
Sarah Peyton distinguishes between empathy and resonance: empathy is only your one-way feeling toward someone else, requiring no words or conversation; resonance demands back-and-forth—you ask 'Do I understand you?' through tone, expression, and guessing, and the other person answers 'yes' or 'no.' This bidirectional confirmation is what children truly need.

17:40 Saying 'you're not sad' breaks the nervous system's transmission
When a child expresses an emotion only to have it denied—Sarah Peyton's mother once replied 'You're not sad' when she said 'I'm sad'—it's like installing a broken transmission in the child: the coordination between body and brain that manages stress and restores calm gets destroyed. Without that coordination, the child can only cope by making the nervous system increasingly shut down and cautious about speaking, to handle a world they don't understand and aren't understood in.

24:56 A truly understanding presence rewires how the vagus nerve reacts
Drawing on James Coan's hand-holding research at the University of Virginia: when someone who truly understands you is present, your brain changes how it responds to stress—the hill becomes less steep, effort feels less effortful, pain hurts less. Conversely, if you can narrate your emotions during an accident—'I'm afraid, I'm angry, I'm numb, I'm worried about my child'—that proves you've been 'put into words' by others many times before. If you can't speak it, that experience locks itself into your amygdala and body, never becoming a narrative you can digest.

40:43 Three insecure attachments, three root systems, three growth patterns
Sarah Peyton compares the three insecure attachment styles to three root systems: ambivalent attachment like roots with unpredictable watering, sometimes blooming, sometimes withering; avoidant attachment like roots shut off from all nourishment and joy, eventually developing an insulating layer around the nervous system that stops reaching outward; anxious-resistant attachment like roots that must constantly cling to others to get nutrients, creating deeper rather than lighter dependence on others. A child entering daycare where they must compete with 11 peers for attention can be pushed from avoidant to anxious-resistant—the squeaky wheel gets the grease.

50:17 You can earn secure attachment later, but old patterns persist
Asked whether an insecurely attached parent can still offer their child secure attachment, Sarah Peyton's answer is yes—but not a clean slate. Learning this neurobiology and language, holding warm curiosity toward your child's experience, gives you 'earned secure attachment'—like wrapping your originally avoidant, chaotic, or anxious attachment in a halo of light. The old patterns stay inside, but you can spot them and adjust them with humor, rather than being led by them.

55:35 When children say 'I won't, but I will,' their needs have been heard
In Inbal Kashtan's book, a three-year-old told to stop stomping said 'I don't want to, but I will'—because 'you don't want me to.' Sarah Peyton initially thought her house would never see this, but after three years of asking her children 'Are you willing?' using nonviolent communication, both her older and younger son said nearly the same words to her on the same day. This shows that when parents' needs are truly taken seriously, children's needs start mattering to their parents—but this shift comes slowly, built year after year.

item.title: The Ice Bucket Challenge Raised $220 Million, Yet ALS Still Has No Cure
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-tpwky-冰桶挑战筹了2-2亿美元-als依然没有能治愈的药/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-29-tpwky-冰桶挑战筹了2-2亿美元-als依然没有能治愈的药/
item.description: The 2014 ice bucket challenge drew donations from nearly 30 million people, raising $220 million. Yet more than a decade later, riluzole, the only widely approved drug, extends median survival by just three months.
item.content:encoded:
The 2014 ice bucket challenge drew donations from nearly 30 million people, raising $220 million. Yet more than a decade later, riluzole, the only widely approved drug, extends median survival by just three months.

Three generations of family disease, Lou Gehrig's farewell address, and ALS's still-unsolved mechanisms interweave medical history and science densely.

3:18 Before opening the envelope, he both has the disease and doesn't
Mark Hopkins's great-uncle, uncle, and father all died of ALS, but the only known genetic test at the time—SOD1—came back negative for his uncle and father, leaving the family uncertain for 16 years whether they carried familial ALS. By 2023, ice bucket challenge research funding had enabled discovery of more causative genes, and his father's DNA was retested, revealing a C9ORF72 mutation. This qualified Mark for predictive genetic testing. Under international protocol, results stay on paper, not in electronic medical records, to prevent genetic discrimination. At his final consultation, even the medical geneticist doesn't know the result; the answer is sealed in an envelope, and he can change his mind before opening it.

10:22 Diagnosis by elimination: no single test is definitive
ALS has no specific biomarker and is diagnosed entirely clinically, based on symptoms. Electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction testing don't confirm ALS—they rule out other diseases, like brain tumors or demyelinating disorders, the ALS mimics. This raises an open question the episode keeps returning to: Is ALS one disease, or several different diseases lumped under one name? No one can say for certain.

16:31 Weakness and twitching: two neural systems sending different alarms
ALS damages both motor neuron systems. Upper motor neuron injury (brain to spinal cord) causes weakness, hyperactive reflexes, increased muscle tone, and spasticity—the brain's inhibitory signal to the spinal cord is lost. Lower motor neuron injury (spinal cord to muscle) causes atrophy and fasciculations—the muscle loses all nerve supply. About 60% of patients have spinal onset first (limb weakness); 30% have bulbar onset (speech and swallowing difficulty, tongue atrophy), which typically signals more severe disease and faster progression. Nearly all patients eventually develop both types of symptoms.

25:53 90% of patients have no family history
Only 5–15% of ALS cases are familial, but no single gene is responsible—at least 20 known related genes exist, with new papers suggesting up to 40. Most follow autosomal dominant inheritance, like Huntington's disease or frontotemporal dementia; theoretically, a single mutation copy carries risk, but penetrance is not 100%, complicating genetic counseling—having the gene doesn't guarantee disease. Conversely, 85–90% of patients have no family history (sporadic cases); some test positive for the same genes found in familial cases, but not all do.

26:54 95% of patients have the same protein piling up in their brains—no one knows why
In 95% of ALS patients, TDP-43 protein accumulates abnormally in neurons—normally confined to the cell nucleus, it migrates to the cytoplasm and forms clumps. The known related genes involve RNA/DNA metabolism, membrane transport, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, and other pathways, but no one can explain the mechanism. Erin Welsh posed the key question: Is this protein aggregation and genetic abnormality the cause of ALS, or a consequence of disease progression? The answer remains unknown.

34:07 Two approved drugs, and even doctors can't explain why they work
Only two drugs have been approved specifically for ALS: Riluzole extends median survival by approximately three months and is the most widely approved globally. Edaravone helps only a subset of patients (typically those with faster progression) and is FDA-approved but not approved in most of Europe. Tofersen, a gene therapy approved in 2023, targets a specific gene and went through accelerated review; trials are still ongoing, and there is no clear evidence yet that it improves survival or slows progression. What has consistently proven to improve quality of life and survival is coordinated multidisciplinary care—physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, nutrition, respiratory care, social work, and palliative care—though not all patients can access these resources.

48:41 After 2,130 consecutive games, he missed for the first time
Lou Gehrig played consecutive games from June 2, 1925 until April 30, 1939—2,130 games—a record that stood until Cal Ripken Jr. broke it in the 1990s, earning Gehrig the nickname Iron Horse. During the 1939 season, his hitting and fielding visibly declined; the team physician initially suspected a gallbladder problem, but the Mayo Clinic diagnosed ALS. The diagnosing doctor could recognize it instantly because his own mother had died of the disease years before. After the diagnosis became public, the team held Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day. He delivered a farewell speech at Yankee Stadium that became known as baseball's Gettysburg Address. Gehrig died on June 2, 1941, at age 37, less than two years after his diagnosis.

1:06:02 Ice bucket challenge raised $220 million and got no miracle drug
The 2014 ice bucket challenge was popularized by Pete Frates, a former Boston College baseball player. Over 17 million people uploaded videos, generating more than 10 billion views and reaching approximately 500 million people. By summer's end, over 28 million donors had contributed, raising roughly $220 million globally—far exceeding typical annual ALS research budgets. More than a decade later, no game-changing drug has emerged. What impressed Erin was ALS Untangled, founded in 2009 by the North American ALS Research Group. It systematically reviews alternative therapies and off-label medications circulating online and publishes peer-reviewed assessments, helping patients and families with limited standard options who might otherwise turn to unproven treatments find evidence-based information.

item.description: When your child is excluded from their friend group, the instinct to reconcile or confront the other parents usually backfires. What matters is handling your own anger first, then asking what your child wants to do about it.
item.content:encoded:
When your child is excluded from their friend group, the instinct to reconcile or confront the other parents usually backfires. What matters is handling your own anger first, then asking what your child wants to do about it.

This episode walks through a real listener letter, breaking down how middle-school girl cliques operate and when they turn exclusionary—packed with practical scripts, though you can skip the sponsor reads.

0:00 Exclusion is chemical, not personal: once a foursome locks in, anyone becomes the excluded one
Every middle-schooler is like an atom trying to fit into a ‘compound’—a friend group. Once four kids form a stable group, they will exclude the outsider even if they are individually warm with her during lunch, weekends, or class. The group's stability depends on staying exactly four. Adding anyone shifts the chemistry. This reframe helps an excluded kid see exclusion as mechanical, not a personal attack.

10:24 Excluding her is not personal attack; it is kids choosing which tribe to join
This stage is what Michelle calls ‘bellying up to the buffet’—suddenly, kids realize their choice of friends signals who they are to everyone else. Some kids are still in a butter-noodles-and-chicken-nuggets phase, and that is fine. But other kids think ‘pepperoni pizza is cooler,’ so they cluster around emerging tastes and broadcast ‘I'm more mature, more cool.’ It is not a coordinated attack on anyone. It is every kid answering ‘who am I’ by choosing who to stand next to.

12:30 Those hot-and-cold friends are confused about their own feelings, not being fake
The most puzzling detail in the letter: the girls who exclude her at school invite her over on weekends to play with American Girl dolls. That is not hypocrisy—those girls genuinely like her and genuinely want to be cool at school at the same time. Michelle quotes her cousin: if you cannot read how someone feels about you, they probably cannot read it themselves either. That inner conflict is closer to the truth than any moral scorecard.

14:32 Stepping in to negotiate closes the door that might have opened by itself
Michelle warns against jumping in with ‘you grew up together, you should work this out’-style pressure. It almost always backfires. By high school, these girls might naturally find their way back, drawn by new shared interests—if a parent has not torched the ground first. Lisa adds: kids experience 40 dimensions of social complexity; they perceive 20; adults understand maybe 2. Steering their friendships from a 2-dimensional view is like a blind person directing traffic.

15:32 Think of the clique like your friend's ex: taking sides now risks awkwardness later
Lisa offers a tool for managing your own anger: think of the hot-and-cold girls as your friend's ex-boyfriend. You can hold your friend's pain, but if you pile on—‘I never liked him anyway’—you have just signaled that her feelings never mattered to you. And if they get back together, you are awkward. Same logic: these 13-year-olds are probably not villains, and they could easily become friends again in six months. Your job is restraint, not taking sides.

17:36 When your child asks what is wrong with her, do not rush to fix it
When your child breaks down asking ‘am I the problem,’ do not panic-solve with ice cream, a new friend, or trash-talking the other girls. That teaches her to outsource pain instead of feeling through it. Better: ask ‘what would help?’ and let her answer—step back from Snapchat, stay home and watch a movie, go find other people. The message is ‘this sucks and you can handle it and I am here’—not ‘this is too big for you.’

20:47 Your adult friendship and your child's peer world are two separate systems
The harder case: the girls in the clique are the children of your friends. Both guests agree—do not end your adult friendship because of kid drama, but also do not force your child to attend family events to patch up your friendship. Keep them on parallel tracks. Lisa admits she deliberately does not befriend her kids' friends' parents. But she warns: if your only friendships run through your kids, that is not fair to them. Adults need their own world.

25:54 The painful middle years are where resilient adults learn to land on their feet
Michelle closes with her sharpest line: what looks like a curse now may look like a blessing later. She has watched adults look back and realize that 13 to 15—the years they felt invisible and unwanted—taught them how to make friends from scratch and build real interests. Kids who never taste rejection, who never have a friendship break, hit adulthood more fragile. The pain is the practice ground. Resilience is not given; it is built.

item.description: Two mothers tried a counterintuitive suggestion: name the loss at transitions instead of soothing, distracting, or comforting. After weeks, both their children's door-slamming meltdowns and hair-pulling self-soothing noticeably decreased.
item.content:encoded:
Two mothers tried a counterintuitive suggestion: name the loss at transitions instead of soothing, distracting, or comforting. After weeks, both their children's door-slamming meltdowns and hair-pulling self-soothing noticeably decreased.

This episode is a listener follow-up with no new theory, but real results proving that naming feelings is genuinely effective, not indulgent.

4:11 Door-slamming meltdowns emerge within three weeks of school transfer
One mother noticed her 4-year-old daughter saying goodbye happily at her previous school. After transferring to the same school where the mother teaches, the situation deteriorated within three weeks: first, complaints about the cafeteria being too loud and cold; then crying and chasing to the door; finally kicking, biting, and slamming the glass door. The school has asked the mother to skip early pick-up this week.

5:11 Visibility without access: the harder problem than simple separation
Janet highlights an unspoken dynamic the mother hadn't articulated: being in the same building as your primary attachment figure but having no access to her is harder than separation for a determined child. The mother confirmed that discussing this openly, plus letting her daughter choose which door to exit through and get a kiss goodbye, noticeably improved pick-ups. Her older sister began helping with classroom tasks.

7:15 Toddlers resort to hair-pulling when family transitions extend for weeks
A second mother writes that her 21-month-old daughter pulls her hair to self-soothe during frustration, exhaustion, or boredom. The family is managing a life transition that will last another 4–6 weeks. She's already coaching her daughter to say "I'm frustrated," and has tried ice rings, string toys, and pacifiers. But she admits it "really bothers me" to watch.

8:16 Naming the transition's difficulty visibly reduced meltdowns in both families
Janet gives both mothers identical counsel: speak directly to the hardship ("this change is hard," "you might miss the way things were") rather than instinctively soothing, distracting, or reassuring. The point isn't to elicit an answer—it's to let the child feel witnessed. Both mothers report back: naming the feeling itself noticeably reduced hair-pulling and pick-up meltdowns.

12:21 Parents' language shapes the emotion more than the event does
Janet raises a subtler mechanism: when a child reacts intensely, anxious parents often label it—"you're scared," "you're angry," "you're so upset you're falling apart"—but the child may have only been startled or surprised, something far milder. Parental language teaches children to inhabit emotions larger than reality warrants.

14:30 Replacing "scared" with specifics lets children approach what they feared
This mother realized "scared" and "afraid" were nearly her daughter's only emotion vocabulary. Reflecting those words back each time was cementing the fear. She shifted to "that bird startled you" or "that's a loud sound" instead of "you're scared." Her daughter stopped reporting fear as often and began approaching things she'd previously avoided—like walking past the parking lot hand-in-hand instead of asking to be carried.

15:31 When meltdowns are truly intense, the guidance becomes less clear
One mother raises a question Janet sidestepped: when the reaction is truly intense—shrieking, hard crying—should she still keep it measured ("wow, you really don't like that") while calmly scooping her up, or shift to something weightier? She hasn't yet figured out the right calibration for genuine meltdowns.

18:33 Witnessing and holding space, not fixing: the parent's real job
Janet's answer: children don't need parents to hit the perfect phrase or diagnose the emotion precisely. Often they need nothing but space to fully release the feeling, with parents ready to pick her up, or not, or simply let her cry on the floor. She frames the role as "present, caring, empathetic, but not here to fix the problem"—something that requires a lifetime of practice.
